screens.title: Launch Files and System Orchestration
screens.narratorSegment: In real ROS development you rarely start every node by hand. Launch files let you describe a complete system — nodes, parameters, remappings, and included modules — in one XML document. In this chapter you will learn the core tags and patterns used in launch files, how to pass arguments and load YAML parameters, and how to compose larger systems using includes. This matters because a correct launch file turns a multi-step manual startup into a single, repeatable command. For example, you can set a robot name, load sensor parameters, start state publishers, and open RViz with one roslaunch invocation. You will also learn common errors and how to debug them by inspecting node output and verifying paths. By the end you should be able to write a launch file that starts a publisher, a subscriber, remaps a topic, and includes a prewritten launch file. Think about a scenario where you need to run a simulator and a real sensor bridge together; a launch file is the safe and repeatable way to compose those systems. What single launch command would you use to start your robot next time?

Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › Launch Files and System Orchestration
Launch Files and System Orchestration
Start, configure, and compose ROS nodes through XML launch files
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
What you'll master

Write launch XML that starts multiple nodes, loads YAML params, remaps topics, and composes includes so one command boots an entire system.

Why it matters

Repeatability and debugging: you run the same configuration each time and see node output centrally with output="screen".

You will also be able to pass command-line arguments to a launch file and use the $(find package_name) substitution to keep paths portable. Finally, you will know how to run a complete multi-node ROS system with a single roslaunch command and how to diagnose and fix common launch errors such as missing packages, wrong executable names, permission problems, and remap mistakes. screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Checks
screens.narratorSegment: In addition to writing launch files, you will practice verification steps that reveal configuration problems early. You will learn to run roslaunch and then use rosnode list to confirm nodes are active and rosparam list and get to inspect parameters on the parameter server. You will use output="screen" in development so node errors surface in the terminal immediately. When a node fails to start, you will know to check that the package exists and that the executable name and permissions are correct. You will also practice using remap tags to connect packages that use different topic names without changing their source code. These verification skills are important because launch files can hide assumptions: a missing YAML path or a wrong package name will make the system incomplete. The rhythm of write, launch, inspect logs, and adjust will be your daily workflow for composing stable ROS systems.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › Learning Objectives — Practical Checks
Verification and Debugging Objectives
Commands and habits to validate a launched system
Check nodes

Use rosnode list to confirm each expected node is running after roslaunch.

Inspect params

Use rosparam list and rosparam get to verify parameter names and values loaded by <rosparam> or <param>.

Surface errors

Use output="screen" during development so startup failures are visible in the terminal logs.

Common mistake

Using the wrong executable name in the type attribute or forgetting chmod +x causes a node to immediately die. Check permissions and type spelling first.

Pro tip

Start with a minimal launch that sets a single node and parameter, confirm it runs, then expand by including additional launch files.

screens.title: What is a launch file?
screens.narratorSegment: A launch file is an XML document that describes how to start and configure a ROS system. At its root is the launch tag which contains node entries, parameter settings, rosparam file loads, remappings, and include directives. The value of a launch file is repeatability: instead of running roscore and multiple nodes by hand, you write the configuration once and run roslaunch my_package my_file. launch to reproduce the same system. For example, you might set a global parameter robot_name, load a YAML containing sensor calibration, launch a state publisher, start sensor drivers, and open RViz — all from the same file. A common misconception is that launch files replace debugging; they do not. They make debugging easier by exposing node output when output="screen" and by providing a single place to inspect configuration. Another misconception is that launch files must be large; it's better to compose small reusable launch files and include them. In practice you will store launch files in the launch/ directory of a package with a. launch extension so roslaunch can find them. How you organize tags and includes determines how maintainable your orchestration becomes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › What is a launch file?
Definition

Launch file explained

An XML file saved in a package's launch/ directory that describes nodes, parameters, and composition rules. It is executed with roslaunch to bring up a full system.

Why use it
Automates startup, captures config, simplifies experiments.
Where to put it
Package root under launch/ with a .launch extension.
Key Takeaway

A launch file is the reproducible recipe to start and configure all parts of a robot system so you avoid manual startup steps.

Analogy & Example
Analogy
Think of a launch file as a recipe: ingredients are nodes and parameters, the steps are launch directives, and includes are reusable sub-recipes.
Concrete example (snippet)
<launch>
  <param name="robot_name" value="my_robot" />
  <node pkg="my_first_robot" type="my_first_node.py" name="robot_publisher" output="screen" />
</launch>
Misconception
Launch files hide errors — actually they surface them if you use output="screen" and inspect logs.
Pro tip
Keep launch files small. Use <include> to compose larger systems from reusable pieces.

screens.title: Core tags: <launch>, <node>, <param>, <rosparam>
screens.narratorSegment: The most used tags in a launch file are the root launch, node for starting executables, param for single parameter settings, and rosparam for loading structured YAML files. The launch tag wraps everything. The node tag needs attributes: pkg points to the package, type names the executable or script, name sets the ROS node name, and output controls whether messages appear on screen. Use param inside launch for global parameters or inside node for private parameters that belong to that node's namespace. rosparam is used when you have many related parameters in a YAML file — load them with command="load" so the parameter server receives multiple entries at once. A concrete example is setting robot_description using rosparam file path to a URDF textfile. A common mistake is confusing param and rosparam: param sets a single key and value, while rosparam loads a whole file or dumps many keys. When you launch, prefer output="screen" during development to see stack traces and immediate errors. Remember to make Python scripts executable and verify type paths with the executable name exactly as installed in the package.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › Core tags
Code walkthrough
node, param, and rosparam in practice
<launch>
  <param name="robot_name" value="my_robot" />
  <rosparam file="$(find my_first_robot)/config/robot_config.yaml" command="load" />

  <node pkg="my_first_robot" type="my_first_node.py" name="robot_publisher" output="screen" />
</launch>
<node>
Starts an executable: pkg, type, name, output, respawn, required, ns.
<param>
Sets a single parameter on the Parameter Server. Can be global or private to a node.
<rosparam>
Loads or dumps YAML files. Use when you have many structured parameters.
Key Takeaway

Use param for single settings and rosparam for structured YAML; node ties code to package and runtime options.

Common mistake

Forgetting to make Python executables executable or using the wrong type name causes immediate node death.

Example scenario

Load sensor calibration from YAML with <rosparam file="path" command="load"/>, then set node private parameters inside its <node> block for driver tuning. Verify with rosparam list and rosparam get.

Misconception check

Do not assume param and rosparam are interchangeable. If you need nested structures or many keys, use rosparam to avoid many repetitive <param> tags.

screens.title: Arguments and substitutions
screens.narratorSegment: Arguments let you parameterize a launch file so the same file can start different configurations. Use the arg tag to define a name and a default value, then use $(arg name) to substitute its value in param tags or node attributes. This pattern is useful when you want to change a robot name, toggle simulation mode, or pass sensor frequencies without editing the file. For example, define robot_name and simulation defaults, then set param entries that use $(arg robot_name). When you run roslaunch, pass new values like robot_name:=turtlebot_01 simulation:=false to override defaults. A practical workflow is to define sensible defaults in the launch and override them from CI scripts or command line during testing. A common misconception is that args are global environment variables; they are local to the launch invocation and only affect substitution points that use $(arg). Another pitfall is misnaming the arg when substituting — any misspelling leads to unresolved references. As you compose large systems, use args to keep included launch files configurable and portable. Arguments and substitutions means use <arg> and $(arg name) to make launch files configurable without editing xml, and pass values at launch time.. In practical terms, make launch files configurable from the command line. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › Arguments and substitutions
Process
Define, substitute, and override
Step 1 — Define args
<arg name="robot_name" default="my_robot" />
Step 2 — Use $(arg)
Substitute with $(arg robot_name) in <param> or node attributes.
Step 3 — Override
Launch: roslaunch pkg file.launch robot_name:=turtlebot_01
Key Takeaway

Args let you write one launch file that supports multiple runtime configurations. Override defaults from the command line during testing and deployment.

Pitfall

Misspelling an arg name in $(arg) is silent and leads to unresolved substitution. Keep names consistent.

screens.title: <param> vs <rosparam>
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding when to use param versus rosparam keeps your launch files clean and efficient. Use param when you need to set a single key-value pair, for example setting max_speed or a boolean flag like use_imu. Param is quick and explicit and can live inside a node block to make the parameter private to that node. Use rosparam when you have many parameters organized in a YAML file — for example sensor calibration, controller gains, or a robot description. rosparam file="path" command="load" loads a structured set of keys into the parameter server so the node can read them without multiple individual declarations. The common error is to attempt to represent nested YAML structures with multiple param tags; that becomes verbose and error-prone. Another important difference is that rosparam supports dump and load for saving and restoring the server state. In practice you will combine both: small tuning values as params and complex sets as rosparam-loaded YAML. Verify values with rosparam get and rosparam list after launching. <param> vs <rosparam> means <param> is for single values; <rosparam> loads complex structured data from yaml files.. In practical terms, when to use a single param or load a yaml file. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › <param> vs <rosparam>
Use <param>
Single settings

Example: <param name="max_speed" value="1.5" /> inside a node block makes that parameter private to the node's namespace if needed.

When to choose
Quick, explicit values and node-scoped settings.
Use <rosparam>
Load structured YAML

Example: <rosparam file="$(find my_first_robot)/config/robot_config.yaml" command="load" /> loads many structured keys for sensors or controllers.

When to choose
Use when parameters are numerous or nested; avoids many repeated <param> tags.
Key Takeaway

Prefer <param> for single values and <rosparam> to load structured YAML files for clarity and maintainability.

Common mistake

Using many <param> tags for nested structures becomes error-prone; prefer a single <rosparam> load.

Verify

After launch, use rosparam list and rosparam get to confirm values were loaded correctly.

screens.title: <remap> and name spaces
screens.narratorSegment: Remapping allows you to translate topic or service names so two packages that use different names can interoperate without modifying either package's source. The remap tag uses from and to attributes. For example, if one package publishes on /cmd_vel and another subscribes to /robot/cmd_vel, you can add a remap inside the node that runs the subscriber: <remap from="/robot/cmd_vel" to="/cmd_vel" />. Namespaces further structure topics: use ns="robot1" on a node to scope all its names under /robot1/. A subtle misconception is thinking remaps change the publisher's global name; instead they affect the node instance in which the remap is applied. Remaps are evaluated when the node starts and only affect that node's view of names. Use remapping to compose third-party packages: you can run the same binaries under different namespaces and remap their topics to avoid collisions. Always verify topic names with rostopic list and rostopic echo to ensure remaps produced the intended mapping. <remap> and name spaces means use <remap from="a" to="b"/> and node namespaces to reconcile different naming conventions without editing package code.. In practical terms, connect packages without changing their source code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › Remap and namespaces
Comparison
How remap and namespace interact
Remap example
<node pkg="my_first_robot" type="my_first_node.py" name="remapped_node" output="screen">
  <remap from="/old_topic" to="/new_topic" />
</node>
Namespace example
<node pkg="pkg" type="node.py" name="driver" ns="robot1" />
# node topics become /robot1/...
Key Takeaway

Use remap to reconcile naming differences and namespaces to scope nodes, avoiding code changes when composing packages.

Common mistake

Applying a remap in one node does not change other nodes. Remaps are local to the node's launch context.

Verify

After launching, use rostopic list and rostopic echo to confirm the remapped topics exist and carry the expected messages. If not, verify node names and namespace scopes.

Scenario

When integrating third-party packages, remap topics instead of modifying their code so upgrades remain straightforward.

screens.title: <include> and composing systems
screens.narratorSegment: Include lets you compose larger systems from smaller reusable launch files. Use the include tag with file="$(find package)/launch/file. launch" to embed another launch file. You can pass arguments into included files by nesting arg tags inside the include element. This pattern keeps your top-level launch concise: include sensors. launch, navigation. launch, and visualization. launch rather than repeating nodes. A practical example is a robot main launch that includes sensors, state publishers, and navigation; each included file defines its own nodes and parameters and can accept args for frequencies or namespaces. One misconception is assuming includes merge namespaces automatically; included files run in the including launch's context unless explicitly namespaced. To avoid conflicts, design includes to accept args for namespace and device names. When debugging composition, isolate the included file and run it directly to verify its behavior before including it in a larger orchestration. <include> and composing systems means use <include file="..."> and pass args to build modular, maintainable launch hierarchies.. In practical terms, build larger launch files by including reusable pieces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.2 › Full example
Code example
my_system.launch
<launch>
  <param name="robot_name" value="my_robot" />
  <param name="simulation_mode" value="true" />

  <rosparam file="$(find my_first_robot)/config/robot_config.yaml" command="load" />

  <node pkg="my_first_robot" type="my_first_node.py" name="robot_publisher" output="screen" />
  <node pkg="my_first_robot" type="my_first_node.py" name="robot_subscriber" output="screen" />

  <node pkg="my_first_robot" type="my_first_node.py" name="remapped_node" output="screen">
    <remap from="/old_topic" to="/new_topic" />
  </node>

  <node pkg="my_first_robot" type="my_first_node.py" name="param_node" output="screen">
    <param name="max_speed" value="1.5" />
    <param name="use_imu" value="true" />
  </node>
</launch>
Run and verify

Use roslaunch my_first_robot my_system.launch, then rosnode list and rosparam list to confirm nodes and parameters are active.

Debugging tip

If you see permission denied, make the Python script executable. If roslaunch cannot find a package, source your workspace's setup.bash.

screens.title: $(find package_name) substitution
screens.narratorSegment: The $(find package_name) substitution evaluates to the absolute path of an installed ROS package. Because workspaces and build trees vary between systems, using $(find) keeps launch files portable: you can reference files in a package's config, rviz, or urdf directories without hard-coding absolute paths. For example, $(find my_robot)/urdf/robot. urdf points to the URDF regardless of where the catkin workspace lives. A common misconception is thinking $(find) resolves at parse time only; it is resolved by roslaunch when the file is processed and requires that the package be discoverable via the ROS_PACKAGE_PATH. If you get a cannot find package error, the usual fix is to source the workspace's devel/setup. bash so the package path is registered. When writing launch files, prefer $(find) for references to package resources and avoid embedding user-specific absolute paths. This practice increases shareability and reduces path-related errors during deployment or collaboration. $(find package_name) substitution means use $(find package_name) to reference package resources without hard-coded absolute paths, keeping launch files portable.. screens.title: Common launch file errors and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: Several common errors recur when working with launch files. "Cannot find package" means the package is not on ROS_PACKAGE_PATH; the typical fix is to source your workspace's setup. bash and rebuild if necessary. "Cannot find executable" points to an incorrect type attribute or a non-executable script — verify the filename and run chmod +x on Python scripts. "Permission denied" is resolved the same way by setting execute permissions. "Node dies immediately" requires inspecting runtime output; use output="screen" to see the stack trace or log messages. "Topic not found" usually means a remap mistake or that a publisher hasn't started; verify topic names and remaps with rostopic list. When diagnosis is unclear, isolate the failing node by creating a small launch that runs only that node and necessary parameters. Keep unit-tested smaller includes so faults are easier to locate. These debugging habits will save time and make launch-based orchestration reliable in practice. Common errors and fixes
A checklist for diagnosing launch failures
Cannot find package
Source your workspace's setup.bash and ensure the package is built and in ROS_PACKAGE_PATH.
Cannot find executable
Check the type attribute and make Python scripts executable with chmod +x.
Node dies immediately
Use output="screen" to see logs; run the node directly to reproduce the error.
Topic not found
Verify remaps and that the publisher has started; use rostopic list and echo.
Pro tip

Start small. Verify each include or node independently before composing them to reduce search space for bugs.

When stuck

Run failing nodes directly from the terminal to see full tracebacks and environment errors that roslaunch might hide.

fullNarratorScript:
In real ROS development you rarely start every node by hand. Launch files let you describe a complete system — nodes, parameters, remappings, and included modules — in one XML document. In this chapter you will learn the core tags and patterns used in launch files, how to pass arguments and load YAML parameters, and how to compose larger systems using includes. This matters because a correct launch file turns a multi-step manual startup into a single, repeatable command. For example, you can set a robot name, load sensor parameters, start state publishers, and open RViz with one roslaunch invocation. You will also learn common errors and how to debug them by inspecting node output and verifying paths. By the end you should be able to write a launch file that starts a publisher, a subscriber, remaps a topic, and includes a prewritten launch file. Think about a scenario where you need to run a simulator and a real sensor bridge together; a launch file is the safe and repeatable way to compose those systems. What single launch command would you use to start your robot next time?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to write XML launch files that start multiple nodes, set parameters, remap topic names, and include other launch files for composition. You will understand the purpose and usage of the core tags: launch, node, param, rosparam, remap, include, and arg. You will also be able to pass command-line arguments to a launch file and use the $(find package_name) substitution to keep paths portable. Finally, you will know how to run a complete multi-node ROS system with a single roslaunch command and how to diagnose and fix common launch errors such as missing packages, wrong executable names, permission problems, and remap mistakes. These skills let you automate startup, reproduce experiments, and reduce manual errors when testing robots or simulations. As you practice, focus on clear naming, sensible namespaces, and using output="screen" to surface runtime errors for debugging. Think of a launch file as the orchestration recipe that makes complex systems easy to run reliably.

In addition to writing launch files, you will practice verification steps that reveal configuration problems early. You will learn to run roslaunch and then use rosnode list to confirm nodes are active and rosparam list and get to inspect parameters on the parameter server. You will use output="screen" in development so node errors surface in the terminal immediately. When a node fails to start, you will know to check that the package exists and that the executable name and permissions are correct. You will also practice using remap tags to connect packages that use different topic names without changing their source code. These verification skills are important because launch files can hide assumptions: a missing YAML path or a wrong package name will make the system incomplete. The rhythm of write, launch, inspect logs, and adjust will be your daily workflow for composing stable ROS systems.

A launch file is an XML document that describes how to start and configure a ROS system. At its root is the launch tag which contains node entries, parameter settings, rosparam file loads, remappings, and include directives. The value of a launch file is repeatability: instead of running roscore and multiple nodes by hand, you write the configuration once and run roslaunch my_package my_file. launch to reproduce the same system. For example, you might set a global parameter robot_name, load a YAML containing sensor calibration, launch a state publisher, start sensor drivers, and open RViz — all from the same file. A common misconception is that launch files replace debugging; they do not. They make debugging easier by exposing node output when output="screen" and by providing a single place to inspect configuration. Another misconception is that launch files must be large; it's better to compose small reusable launch files and include them. In practice you will store launch files in the launch/ directory of a package with a. launch extension so roslaunch can find them. How you organize tags and includes determines how maintainable your orchestration becomes.

The most used tags in a launch file are the root launch, node for starting executables, param for single parameter settings, and rosparam for loading structured YAML files. The launch tag wraps everything. The node tag needs attributes: pkg points to the package, type names the executable or script, name sets the ROS node name, and output controls whether messages appear on screen. Use param inside launch for global parameters or inside node for private parameters that belong to that node's namespace. rosparam is used when you have many related parameters in a YAML file — load them with command="load" so the parameter server receives multiple entries at once. A concrete example is setting robot_description using rosparam file path to a URDF textfile. A common mistake is confusing param and rosparam: param sets a single key and value, while rosparam loads a whole file or dumps many keys. When you launch, prefer output="screen" during development to see stack traces and immediate errors. Remember to make Python scripts executable and verify type paths with the executable name exactly as installed in the package.

Arguments let you parameterize a launch file so the same file can start different configurations. Use the arg tag to define a name and a default value, then use $(arg name) to substitute its value in param tags or node attributes. This pattern is useful when you want to change a robot name, toggle simulation mode, or pass sensor frequencies without editing the file. For example, define robot_name and simulation defaults, then set param entries that use $(arg robot_name). When you run roslaunch, pass new values like robot_name:=turtlebot_01 simulation:=false to override defaults. A practical workflow is to define sensible defaults in the launch and override them from CI scripts or command line during testing. A common misconception is that args are global environment variables; they are local to the launch invocation and only affect substitution points that use $(arg). Another pitfall is misnaming the arg when substituting — any misspelling leads to unresolved references. As you compose large systems, use args to keep included launch files configurable and portable. Arguments and substitutions means use <arg> and $(arg name) to make launch files configurable without editing xml, and pass values at launch time.. In practical terms, make launch files configurable from the command line. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding when to use param versus rosparam keeps your launch files clean and efficient. Use param when you need to set a single key-value pair, for example setting max_speed or a boolean flag like use_imu. Param is quick and explicit and can live inside a node block to make the parameter private to that node. Use rosparam when you have many parameters organized in a YAML file — for example sensor calibration, controller gains, or a robot description. rosparam file="path" command="load" loads a structured set of keys into the parameter server so the node can read them without multiple individual declarations. The common error is to attempt to represent nested YAML structures with multiple param tags; that becomes verbose and error-prone. Another important difference is that rosparam supports dump and load for saving and restoring the server state. In practice you will combine both: small tuning values as params and complex sets as rosparam-loaded YAML. Verify values with rosparam get and rosparam list after launching. <param> vs <rosparam> means <param> is for single values; <rosparam> loads complex structured data from yaml files.. In practical terms, when to use a single param or load a yaml file. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Remapping allows you to translate topic or service names so two packages that use different names can interoperate without modifying either package's source. The remap tag uses from and to attributes. For example, if one package publishes on /cmd_vel and another subscribes to /robot/cmd_vel, you can add a remap inside the node that runs the subscriber: <remap from="/robot/cmd_vel" to="/cmd_vel" />. Namespaces further structure topics: use ns="robot1" on a node to scope all its names under /robot1/. A subtle misconception is thinking remaps change the publisher's global name; instead they affect the node instance in which the remap is applied. Remaps are evaluated when the node starts and only affect that node's view of names. Use remapping to compose third-party packages: you can run the same binaries under different namespaces and remap their topics to avoid collisions. Always verify topic names with rostopic list and rostopic echo to ensure remaps produced the intended mapping. <remap> and name spaces means use <remap from="a" to="b"/> and node namespaces to reconcile different naming conventions without editing package code.. In practical terms, connect packages without changing their source code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Several common errors recur when working with launch files. "Cannot find package" means the package is not on ROS_PACKAGE_PATH; the typical fix is to source your workspace's setup. bash and rebuild if necessary. "Cannot find executable" points to an incorrect type attribute or a non-executable script — verify the filename and run chmod +x on Python scripts. "Permission denied" is resolved the same way by setting execute permissions. "Node dies immediately" requires inspecting runtime output; use output="screen" to see the stack trace or log messages. "Topic not found" usually means a remap mistake or that a publisher hasn't started; verify topic names and remaps with rostopic list.
